plan.contextChunk: This figure is a line graph with two smooth curves showing how the equilibrium composition of a two-isomer mixture depends on the energy difference between the isomers. The plotting field is pale blue with a faint grid. The vertical axis is labeled Percent and runs from 0 to 100 with labels every 20 units. The same horizontal variable is given two scales: the bottom axis, labeled Energy difference (kJ/mol), extends from 0 to 15 with labeled ticks at 5, 10 and 15, while the top axis, labeled Energy difference (kcal/mol), covers 0 to just over 3 with ticks at 0, 1, 2 and 3. Both curves originate together at 50 percent where the energy difference is zero. The blue curve, tagged by a curved leader line to the label More stable isomer, rises steeply at small energy differences and then flattens, passing roughly 90 percent near 6 kJ/mol and approaching 100 percent at the right edge. The magenta curve, similarly tagged Less stable isomer, is its mirror image, dropping steeply and then leveling out at a few percent. The two curves add to 100 at every horizontal position, so a vertical slice anywhere on the plot reads off the population split for that energy gap. The graph attaches numbers to the relationship between a modest energy separation and a strongly lopsided equilibrium mixture.

interactionPlan.concept: The equilibrium ratio of two isomers depends exponentially on their energy difference, so even a modest energy gap produces a strongly lopsided mixture whose percentages always sum to 100.

pale blue plotting field with faint gridlines
blue curve labeled 'More stable isomer' via a curved leader line — starts at 50%, rises steeply, passes ~90% near 6 kJ/mol, approaches 100%

interactions.label: Energy difference
interactions.teaches: How steeply the equilibrium composition shifts with energy gap — the first few kJ/mol do almost all the work, moving the mixture from 50:50 to roughly 90:10, after which additional gap barely changes the percentages

interactions.label: Energy units
interactions.teaches: kJ/mol and kcal/mol are two labels for the same physical energy difference — the equilibrium relationship is unchanged, only the numeric readout of the cursor position converts (÷4.184)

demo_steps.title: Zero gap means 50:50
demo_steps.narration: With no energy difference the isomers are equally stable, so both curves meet at 50% — the equilibrium mixture is an even split.

demo_steps.title: A small gap tips the balance
demo_steps.narration: Drag to about 6 kJ/mol: the more stable isomer already makes up ~90% of the mixture. Notice how little the curves move beyond this point — small energy differences dominate the composition.

demo_steps.title: Same slice, different units
demo_steps.narration: Switch the readout to kcal/mol. The vertical guide and the percentages stay exactly where they were; only the energy number changes, showing both axis scales describe one identical relationship.

demo_steps.title: Large gaps give pure mixtures
demo_steps.narration: Push toward 12–14 kJ/mol: the less stable isomer drops to a few percent or less, so a gap of only ~3 kcal/mol effectively yields a single isomer at equilibrium.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because equilibrium composition responds exponentially to energy difference, a gap of just a few kJ/mol (~1 kcal/mol) already turns a 50:50 mixture into a roughly 75:25 one — small stability differences produce heavily one-sided mixtures.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate as a pale blue plotting field with faint gray gridlines. Percent axis on the left (0–100, ticks every 20). Dual x-axes: bottom in kJ/mol (0–15, labeled at 5/10/15), top in kcal/mol (0–3+, labeled at 0/1/2/3) aligned so 0 and the right edge coincide. Blue curve and magenta curve are exact mirror images about the 50% horizontal line, both starting together at 50% at x=0; shape follows a Boltzmann-style ratio (percent more-stable = 100/(1+exp(-ΔE/RT)) at ~298 K). Labels 'More stable isomer' and 'Less stable isomer' sit on the right side with curved leader arrows pointing to their curves. The slider drives a vertical guide line spanning the plot height, with dots where it crosses each curve and numeric percent readouts that always sum to 100; the energy readout converts units per the toggle without moving the guide.

authoredContext:
You might recall from your general chemistry course that it’s possible to calculate the percentages of two isomers at equilibrium using the equation ΔE = –RT ln K, where ΔE is the energy difference between isomers, R is the gas constant [8.315 J/(K·mol)], T is the Kelvin temperature, and K is the equilibrium constant between isomers. For example, an energy difference of 7.6 kJ/mol means that about 95% of methylcyclohexane molecules have an equatorial methyl group at any given instant while only 5% have an axial methyl group. The figure plots the relationship between energy and isomer percentages.

A plot of the percentages of two isomers at equilibrium versus the energy difference between them. The curves are calculated using the equation ΔE = −RT ln K.

A graph of percent against energy difference in kilojoules per mole plots an increasing curve for more stable isomer and decreasing curve for less stable isomer.

The energy difference between axial and equatorial conformations is due to steric strain caused by 1,3-diaxial interactions. The axial methyl group on C1 is too close to the axial hydrogens three carbons away on C3 and C5, resulting in 7.6 kJ/mol of steric strain (the figure).

discrepancies: The source labels the curves directly with arrows pointing to each curve ('More stable isomer' / 'Less stable isomer'); the generated figure replaces these with a side legend, losing the in-figure annotation style
The source top kcal axis spans 0–3 (matching its bottom 0–15 kJ axis extent); the generated top axis extends to 3.6 and its last tick ('3.6') looks odd and crowds the plot corner
The two '50.0%' readout labels at the default step sit directly on the y-axis at x=0, slightly colliding with the axis/frame
evaluation.notes: Excellent reproduction of the Boltzmann-distribution plot: correct logistic curve shapes, dual kJ/kcal axes, pale blue field, and complementary blue/magenta curves; the slider, step player, unit toggle, and click-to-probe interactions are all functional and pedagogically apt; only the arrow-style in-curve annotations and a slightly off top-axis range differ from the source.
action_items: Add arrow-pointed 'More stable isomer' / 'Less stable isomer' text annotations on the curves (as in the source) instead of relying solely on the side legend
Constrain the top kcal axis to max ≈3 with integer ticks so it mirrors the source's 0–3 range rather than ending at 3.6
Offset the percentage readouts when the guide is at x=0 so the '50.0%' labels do not overlap the y-axis frame
